sources.locator: GNU C Language Introduction and Reference Manual; accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to Enumerations
sources.claim: An enumeration declares named integer constants and an enumerated type, improving domain vocabulary while remaining subject to implementation integer representation rules.

canonicalExplanation.summary: An **enum** gives names to related integer constants: `enum Status { STATUS_PENDING, STATUS_READY, STATUS_FAILED };` (values 0, 1, 2 unless you set them). Code then says `STATUS_READY` instead of a magic `1`. But a C enum is **just an integer underneath**: nothing stops a variable from holding 7, and the compiler won't check it at run time. So pair enums with a `switch` that lists **every enumerator without a `default`**, so that `-Wswitch` (on with -Wall) warns when a new case is added and forgotten. Then handle **invalid values** explicitly after the switch.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
An order system uses `int status` where 0 is pending, 1 ready and 2 failed. A new developer writes `if (status == 3)` for "shipped", which never existed, and a corrupted record with status 7 prints "ready" because of an else branch. enum Status names STATUS_PENDING, STATUS_READY, and STATUS_FAILED so a switch can communicate domain cases clearly. In this lesson you'll use an enum with exhaustive control flow and a safe invalid-value policy.

examples.title: Order status as named cases
examples.situation: enum Status names STATUS_PENDING, STATUS_READY, and STATUS_FAILED so a switch can communicate domain cases clearly.
walkthrough: **enum Status names STATUS_PENDING, STATUS_READY, and STATUS_FAILED:** the magic 0, 1 and 2 disappear.
**So a switch can communicate domain cases clearly:** status_name lists each case by name.
**Invalid policy:** value 7 returns "invalid"; adding STATUS_SHIPPED will make -Wswitch point at every switch to update.
examples.result: Readers see domain words, and new cases can't be silently forgotten.

examples.title: The parsed status
examples.situation: A status arrives as text from a file: "ready". The learner converts it with a cast from an unchecked number.
walkthrough: Parse text into an enum with a function returning bool.
Reject unknown strings instead of casting guesses.
Only validated values ever enter enum Status variables.
examples.result: Invalid input stops at the boundary, not deep in the program.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A C enum is a runtime-checked closed set that can never hold a value outside its listed enumerators.
misconceptions.correction: Enums are integer types. Casts, corrupted data or arithmetic can put any value in them, so code needs an explicit policy for invalid values.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why was enum Status s = 7 accepted?

analogy.example: An enum is like **labelled buttons on a lift panel**: PENDING, READY, FAILED instead of 0, 1, 2. But underneath it's still a number wire: someone can short it to 7, so the lift controller needs a rule for "unknown floor".
limitations: Real panels only have real buttons; enums don't enforce that.
Adding a floor should update every controller: -Wswitch helps.

steps.explanation: The switch communicates each domain case clearly.
Values outside the enum fall to the explicit invalid policy.
Leaving out default makes the compiler flag forgotten cases.

remediation.explanation: For every enum: **name the cases, switch without default, and write what happens for an invalid value.** Convert external data only through a validating parser.

recap.summary: To use enums safely, name domain cases instead of magic numbers, handle every enumerator in switches without a default so -Wswitch catches new cases, add an explicit policy for invalid values afterwards, and validate external data before it becomes an enum.
